Final Project Proposal

Yunwei Zhang

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

From: Yunwei Zhang (GitHub: sherryzyw0120)

Project site: https://sherryzyw0120.github.io/finalproject

What I plan to do

For my final project, I want to work with two of the datasets that come with the course package. The first part looks at whether state background-check laws line up with changes in firearm deaths, using the RAND gun law data (gunleg) together with the CDC firearm mortality data (cdcfiremort). I may also use the CDC homicide data (cdcmurd) as a second outcome. The second part uses the CDC outbreak data (waterborne) to ask whether outbreaks spread in different ways (food, water, person to person) differ in how often people end up in the hospital.

Each part will be its own vignette. I’ll explain where the data came from, show descriptive statistics for the variables I use, state what I’m trying to find out, and write up what I found and what the limitations are. Some steps will be repeated a lot (cleaning, joining, summarizing by state or by year), so I’ll write small R functions for those instead of copying code.

Part 1: Background-check laws and firearm deaths

The data

‘gunleg’ is the RAND State Firearm Law Database, which contains 1,902 rows, with each row representing a different law. For each law, the dataset includes the state, the type of law (out of 20 categories, such as background checks, waiting periods, and child access), whether the law made firearm access more restrictive or permissive, and the dates when it took effect and, if applicable, was replaced. The effective dates range from 1813 to 2025.

‘cdcfiremort’ comes from CDC/NCHS state-level statistics. It includes firearm death rates per 100,000 people and the total number of deaths for each state and DC. The data cover 2005 and 2014 through 2024, giving a total of 612 state-year observations. ‘cdcmurd’ has the same structure but focuses on homicide.

One difference I noticed is that ‘cdcfiremort’ uses full state names, while ‘cdcmurd’ uses two-letter state abbreviations. Since gunleg includes both, I can use it to match the states across the datasets. I’ll also mention the gap between 2005 and 2014 in my write-up, since the data do not cover those years continuously.

Research Question

Do firearm death rates change after a state adopts a restrictive background-check law?

I chose background checks because they are one of the more common law types in the dataset. Between 2015 and 2023, 12 states adopted restrictive background-check laws. Since these years overlap with the firearm death data, I can compare states that adopted these laws with those that did not.

Study Design

Each observation will represent one state in one year from 2014 to 2024. I’ll use the 2005 data for descriptive purposes but leave it out of the regression.

For the exposure, I’ll mark a state as exposed starting the year its first restrictive background-check law took effect. If the law was later replaced or weakened, I’ll update its status. I’ll also test whether starting exposure the following year changes the results. Laws with missing or unclear dates will be excluded from the main analysis.

The main outcome is the firearm death rate per 100,000 people, with homicide rate as a secondary outcome.

I’ll adjust for year, census region, baseline firearm death rate, and the number of other restrictive gun laws already in place.

Methods

First, I’ll organize the law data by state and year and merge it with the death rates. I’ll summarize laws by type and restrictiveness, map background-check laws across states, and compare firearm death trends between adopting and non-adopting states.

For the main analysis, I’ll use a difference-in-differences approach with state and year fixed effects. I’ll also examine trends before and after adoption to see whether the groups followed similar patterns before the laws took effect.

Part 2: Outbreak severity by how the disease spread

The data

waterborne comes from the CDC’s National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS), accessed through the CDC open data API. It contains 66,713 outbreaks from 1971 to 2023, including about 1,069 labeled as “Multistate.”

The dataset includes outbreak year, month, state, transmission mode, and number of illnesses. Many records also report hospitalizations, deaths, causes, and settings, although some information is missing. Hospitalization data are available for about 58,000 records and etiology for around 50,000.

Since the API returns records with different fields, I’ll need to clean the data, convert dates, and identify missing values before analyzing it.

Research Question

Is the way an outbreak spreads associated with its severity, measured by the proportion of infected people who are hospitalized?

Study Design

Each observation will represent one outbreak. I’ll include outbreaks with a known transmission mode and hospitalization count.

The main exposure is transmission mode: person-to-person, foodborne, waterborne, or other. The outcome is the proportion hospitalized out of all reported illnesses. I’ll use hospitalization counts in the model rather than just the calculated percentages.

I’ll adjust for decade, outbreak setting, cause (norovirus, Salmonella, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or other/unknown), and census region. Multistate outbreaks will be treated as a separate geographic group.

I’ll also check whether outbreaks with missing hospitalization data differ from those with complete records.

Methods

I’ll start by summarizing outbreaks, illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths by transmission mode, decade, and region. I’ll compare observed and expected outbreak counts to identify patterns across regions and transmission modes.

For the main analysis, I’ll use binomial or quasi-binomial logistic regression to examine the association between transmission mode and hospitalization proportion while adjusting for the other variables. If possible, I’ll also create an interactive map using leaflet and state.center.

Limitations I expect

Both analyses use observational data, so the results will show associations rather than prove causation.

For Part 1, only 12 states adopted restrictive background-check laws during the study period, which may limit statistical power. States may also differ in other ways, and some may adopt several gun laws around the same time. The gap between 2005 and 2014 also limits the historical comparisons.

For Part 2, the dataset only includes reported outbreaks, and reporting practices have changed over time. Missing hospitalization and cause information could introduce bias. Outbreak severity also depends on the people affected, which may not be fully captured by the available variables.
